_what: Possible patterns: the same kind of thing as the patterns beside them, but ones nobody has proved yet. Each says what is probably happening now, why that is likely, which proved cases sit nearest to it, and what would turn it into cases or knock it down. None of them is evidence, none names a person or a company in the claim, and none is counted in any figure on this map.

items.title: The same drafting shops writing the statutes of many governments at once
items.claim: The text of investment, mining and tax laws is probably supplied to many governments from one small set of drafting shops and model texts, so a rule written by a few unelected people is likely in force in countries that never debated it.
items.rule: The copying is measured one level up. A study of more than 600 bilateral investment treaties found the average treaty takes roughly 50 to 65 per cent of its wording from an earlier one, and over 100 copy 80 per cent or more. The map proves the same movement at the level of statutes: industry-written model bills were copied into about 10,000 United States state bills, and a corporate-and-legislator forum drafted an immigration law that was then enacted. Where text travels by copying, the people who wrote the model also advise the ministry that enacts it.
items.conditions: A bill is often drafted by a few people in one ministry or legislative office, with an outside adviser alongside. The adviser's instructions and drafts are not published, and in most countries there is no register of who wrote a bill. Model texts are public; the drafting advice behind each enactment is not.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'ALEC Exposed: 850 corporate-drafted model bills published' and 'Industry-written model bills copied into 10,000 US state bills', both proved. Also 'ALEC meeting drafted Arizona's SB 1070 immigration law', and the Big Four accountants seconded to the Treasury to help write tax law. Nothing proved yet shows one drafting shop supplying the same operative text to several countries.
items.would_show: Two or more national statutes whose operative provisions match one private model, with an engagement letter, secondment record or drafting file showing the same adviser wrote each.
items.would_refute: Ministry drafting files for the closest-matching statutes showing the text was written in-house, with the model used only as a reference and the adviser excluded from drafting.

items.title: The largest shareholders advising the regulators that oversee them
items.claim: Firms that hold the largest stakes in regulated banks and companies are probably also advising the central banks and finance ministries that set the rules those stakes live under, in several countries at the same time, so one private firm may sit on both sides of the same decision.
items.rule: The structure is documented. One asset manager's advisory arm was created in 2008 to advise governments and central banks, and went on to advise the United States Federal Reserve and several European central banks. Its risk platform was reported to analyse about $21.6 trillion of assets by 2020. Under the Federal Reserve's 2020 facility terms, staff could move from that work to client-facing work after a two-week cooling-off period. The map proves the same arrangement elsewhere: a founder of a finance firm was given a desk inside a government department while the firm was in dealings with it.
items.conditions: These engagements are often awarded without open competition and the contracts are not published. Members of the United States Congress asked in 2020 for the contract terms and conflict-of-interest procedures. The information the adviser sees, such as bank balance sheets under supervisory review or an intervention before it is announced, reaches no other market participant. The safeguards are set and audited by the firm itself.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Greensill Capital: founder inside Downing Street, civil servant on its side', and 'Banker offered Puerto Rico's governor campaign cash to replace his regulator', both proved. Nothing proved yet ties an asset manager's advisory work to a decision that moved its own holdings.
items.would_show: A supervisory, purchase or intervention decision where the record shows the adviser's own holdings or products were affected and its staff drafted or recommended the option chosen.
items.would_refute: Contracts and internal access logs showing the information barriers held, with no traffic between the advisory team and the investment side on the decisions at issue.

items.title: Companies voting the technical standards that become law
items.claim: In the technical committees whose texts national law then adopts by reference, the voting experts are probably in large part employed by the firms the standard governs, so rules with the force of law are likely drafted by the industries they bind.
items.rule: The map proves the mechanism at a standards body. Partners of a software maker joined national committees to vote its document format into the international standard, and a national intelligence agency steered a weakened encryption standard through the standards bodies. The bodies are open to industry by design, and their texts become binding when a government adopts them by reference. A committee that no government controls, whose text becomes law, is the same shape as a lobbyist drafting a bill, which the map proves elsewhere.
items.conditions: Committees run to a few dozen members and are staffed through national standards bodies, many funded by selling the standards they help write. The employer of each voting member, and who paid for each delegate, is generally not stated in the published standard. Drafts and ballots go to members, not to the public.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Microsoft partners joined national committees to vote its format into ISO' and 'NSA steered a weakened encryption standard through NIST and ISO', both proved. Nothing proved yet ties a standard to a member's employer in a way that decided the outcome.
items.would_show: A standard later adopted into national law where the committee record shows the drafting members were employed by firms whose product the text admits or excludes, and a competitor's objection was voted down by those members.
items.would_refute: Committee rosters and ballot records showing government, academic and consumer members held the deciding votes on the standards in question.

items.title: The judges and advocates of investment disputes being one circle
items.claim: The tribunals that decide whether a state may regulate an investor are probably staffed largely from a small circle of people who also argue cases before the same tribunals, so the judges and the advocates in this system may be substantially the same people.
items.rule: This is counted, not supposed. A survey of 1,077 investment arbitrations found 509, or 47 per cent, involved arbitrators who were at the same time acting as counsel or expert in other cases. The system's own rule-writers treat the overlap as a defect: the UNCITRAL working group agreed a code of conduct in 2023 with cooling-off periods of one to three years. The map proves that arbitration itself is a place where influence is bought: a company bribed a government lawyer during an arbitration.
items.conditions: A tribunal is three people, one chosen by each side and one agreed between them, drawn from a small pool of repeat appointees and paid by the parties. Hearings and many awards are confidential. Until the 2023 code, disclosure of concurrent roles was left largely to the arbitrator.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'P&ID bribed a Nigerian government lawyer during arbitration', and 'Leaks say arbitrators weighed bribery of Kazakh officials over Karacha', both proved as bribery in arbitration rather than as double-hatting. Honest gap: no proved case of an arbitrator with concurrent roles shaping an award.
items.would_show: An award where an arbitrator was concurrently counsel for a party, or for its affiliate, in another case on the same treaty provision, and did not disclose it at the time.
items.would_refute: Disclosure records across the same case set showing concurrent roles were declared, and party challenges were heard and ruled on in the closest cases.

items.title: Suppliers and private funders holding seats over what global health buys
items.claim: The bodies that set global health priorities and buy vaccines at scale are probably giving governing seats and funding leverage to the suppliers and private funders who gain from what is bought, so part of the purchaser's agenda may be set by the sellers.
items.rule: The arrangement is published and can be read from the budget. More than 80 per cent of the World Health Organization's budget is voluntary money, and in 2024 to 2025 the largest contributor was a private foundation at about 13 per cent of that. A vaccine alliance was second at about 11.6 per cent, and its board gives permanent seats to the same foundation and to the vaccine industry. The map already proves tobacco companies working inside the WHO. This is the purchasing layer of the same arrangement.
items.conditions: Priorities are set by boards of a few dozen people deciding by consensus or two-thirds majority. Where a body depends on one donor for a large share of its money, withdrawal is a sanction that needs no vote. Supply agreements, prices and volume commitments are routinely confidential.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Tobacco companies secretly worked to undermine WHO from inside', proved as industry inside a rule-making body. Nothing proved yet ties a board seat to a purchase decision.
items.would_show: A procurement or priority decision where the record shows a board member's own product was selected and that member took part in the vote.
items.would_refute: Board minutes and recusal records showing industry and funder seats were excluded from votes on the products they supply.

items.title: Central bankers and the banks they supervise meeting in closed rooms
items.claim: Decisions on money and bank supervision are probably shaped in invitation-only forums where the officials who take them and the bankers they supervise meet without published minutes, moving part of policy out of any record the public can reach.
items.rule: An official watchdog has already found this kind of overlap improper. In January 2018 the European Ombudsman found that a central bank president's membership of an invitation-only bankers' club amounted to maladministration, because members included directors of banks the bank supervised. She recommended he suspend the membership and that future presidents not join. The map proves the older form: bankers secretly drafted the Federal Reserve plan at Jekyll Island, and bank owners bribed a central bank chief in Latvia.
items.conditions: Membership is by invitation and meetings are confidential. Attendance may appear in an official diary, but agendas, papers and discussion do not. The firms in the room are often the ones whose capital, resolution and liquidity support the officials decide.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Bankers secretly drafted the Federal Reserve plan at Jekyll Island', and 'Latvian bank's owners bribed central bank chief and ECB member', both proved. Honest gap: no proved case of a closed-forum meeting shaping a specific rate or supervisory decision.
items.would_show: A supervisory or policy position that changed after a closed meeting, with notes, correspondence or testimony tying the change to what was said there.
items.would_refute: Published agendas and summaries showing the meetings dealt only in general analysis, with matters concerning members' own firms excluded.

items.title: The firms that sell tax structures writing the laws that allow them
items.claim: In jurisdictions that supply secrecy and tax residence to the rest of the world, statutes are probably written in large part by the private firms that then sell the structures those statutes permit, so the law may be drafted by its own customers.
items.rule: Legal scholarship describes interested private parties working closely with the legislatures of small offshore jurisdictions, partners of offshore firms holding government posts, and jurisdictions converting lawmaking authority into revenue. Leak-based reporting found that more than 300 lawyers at one global firm had advised a state or international body on tax or anti-corruption legislation, while the firm was connected to more than 440 offshore companies. The map proves the same pairing in a different setting: accounting-firm staff seconded to a national Treasury to help write tax law.
items.conditions: A small legislature may have no standing drafting office, so an outside draft is often the only draft. The instructing client and fee are not published. The firm that drafts may also incorporate and administer the entities the statute creates, so one firm writes the rule and sells the product.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Big Four accountants seconded to the Treasury to help write tax law', proved as placement inside the body that writes the rule. Honest gap: no proved case of an offshore firm drafting the statute under which it then sells structures.
items.would_show: A statute or amendment whose drafting file, legislative record or billing shows a private firm wrote it, where that firm also sells the structures the statute enables.
items.would_refute: Drafting records showing the text came from a government law office or a multilateral adviser with no commercial interest in the structures created.

items.title: Former intelligence officers selling their service's methods to foreign clients
items.claim: Former officers of national intelligence services are probably working for foreign states and private clients in numbers large enough to matter, carrying the access and methods of the services they left.
items.rule: One case is proved in the form of a United States prosecution agreement. Three former intelligence and military employees ran hacking operations for a foreign government through a company from 2016 to 2019, paid $1.685 million between them, surrendered their clearances and accepted employment limits. Enforcement officials then warned other former employees publicly, which implies the pool is larger than the three charged. The map proves the state-to-state form of the same thing: a state's own service running the access it holds.
items.conditions: These engagements are commercial contracts with non-disclosure terms. Export control is the main legal handle, and it reaches tools more readily than people. There is no public register of where former officers of most services go. The client can classify the work it commissions.
items.documented: Honest zero. The map holds no case of former officers selling their service's methods to a foreign client. Nearest proved: 'CIA and BND secretly owned Swiss cipher firm Crypto AG', which shows a service inside a commercial vendor. The rule above rests on the public prosecution record outside the map.
items.would_show: A second state's enforcement action or court record showing former officers of its own service worked for a foreign client against its interests or its allies.
items.would_refute: Post-employment records showing former officers' foreign work was licensed and supervised, leaving the case isolated rather than typical.

items.title: Suppliers of national identity and payment systems inside the bodies that choose them
items.claim: The companies that build national identity and payment systems are probably inside the ministries and programmes that choose and mandate those systems, so a few suppliers may set the terms on which large populations are enrolled, identified and paid.
items.rule: The map proves the purchasing end of this repeatedly. A multinational paid over $100 million to officials for a $1 billion ID-card deal, and contractors paid a national legislative leader. A Belgian firm was sent to trial over a cut of each passport issued in one country. Identity systems have few qualified bidders, and the lender programmes that fund them publish technical guidance that names vendor lock-in as a risk in borrowing countries.
items.conditions: A national identity decision is usually taken by one commission or ministry, under a single integrator contract running for years. Biometric matching, card supply and payment switching each have few qualified bidders. Contract terms, pricing and data-ownership clauses are often unpublished.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Siemens paid over $100m to Argentine officials for a $1bn ID-card deal', and 'e-KTP contractors paid Indonesia's House Speaker Setya Novanto', both proved as bribery in procurement. Honest gap: no proved case of a supplier writing the specification it then wins.
items.would_show: An identity or payment mandate where the specification was written by a bidder, or the deciding official was employed by one before or after the award.
items.would_refute: Procurement files for the largest such programmes showing specifications written in-house and competitive awards, with deciding officials unconnected to any bidder.
